full_judgment: 7. Basis for applying the principles of acquiescence and waiver is found to be the pre-emptor's knowledge of the sale from the very beginning, his refusal to purchase the land when offered and his inaction and silence when many acts of improvements including construction of dwelling huts. Pre-emptor (P.W.1) said that he was not aware of the sale, nor was the land offered to him by the vendors. But the evidence of OPW 1 belies this claim. As to construction of some dwelling huts in the land, it is found have been admitted by PW 1 during cross-examination. OPW 1 --- who is father of one of the purchasers --- has testified that the pre-emptor had even given assurance that he would not claim pre-emption. This statement has been rejected by him. Mr. Nurullah contends that even if the said offer had been made and the appellant refused to purchase and also gave oral assurance that he would not pre-empt, such an assurance would not constitute "acquiescence or waiver" for, the right of pre-emption did not accrue at this stage but it accrued after the sale. In support of this view, he has referred to a decision of the Nagpur High Court in Govinda Marotisa Vs. Ismail, AIR 1950 Nag. 22. In that case, the pre-emptor, when approached by the vendor to purchase the land, not only refused but also gave assurance to the prospective purchaser that he would not exercise his right of pre-emption, but ultimately after the sale he claimed pre-emption. His claim was resisted on the ground of acquiescence and waiver but it was rejected and pre-emption was allowed.
